chunks.title: About Me: Abdullah Bin Abid
chunks.text:
# About Me: Abdullah Bin Abid

My name is Abdullah Bin Abid. I am a computer science student in my senior year, currently in my 7th semester at the University of Management and Technology (UMT). The area of computer science I care about most is Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning. If a problem can be solved by teaching a model to learn from data, I'm usually all ears.

## Education

I'm doing my bachelor's degree in Computer Science at the University of Management and Technology. I'm in my final year now, in the 7th semester, so the finish line is in sight.

My favourite courses have been Databases and Computer Networks. My least favourite course was Digital Logic Design. Let's just say it was never my cup of tea.

## What I'm interested in

My main interest is AI and machine learning. I've worked on deep learning for image classification, I did an AI research internship, and the AI tools I use most are Claude and Cursor. I've also built full-stack web and mobile apps.

I prefer working on things that haven't been solved yet.

## My goals

After my degree I plan to move abroad, most probably to Canada, to do my master's. After that I hope to get a job in big tech, and I want to start my own startup on the side. I'd rather not put all my eggs in one basket, so the plan is a solid career plus something of my own.

- Designed end-to-end ordering, cart and payment workflows, with integrated analytics tracking revenue, ratings and AR view counts.

chunks.text:
# How I Work, Study and My Advice to Juniors

## When I work best

I'm a night owl. I burn the midnight oil.

## How I study

I'll be honest: these days I'm a last-minute crammer.

## Solo or team

I prefer solo work. That said, I've worked in teams too, and I was team lead on the 3D Food Visualization App.

## My setup

I work on a MacBook. The AI tools I use most are Claude and Cursor. My other everyday tools include Visual Studio, Jupyter Notebooks, Git, MySQL, Node.js and AWS.

## My advice for junior CS students

Do 2 to 3 projects that actually solve significant modern problems. Don't fill your portfolio with tutorials and to-do apps that everyone has built.

## In plain words

I'm a late-night person, I tend to leave studying until close to the deadline, and I like working by myself. My tip for first-year students is to build a small number of meaningful projects that address real present-day challenges instead of many shallow ones.

chunks.title: Project Write-Up: AI Plant Disease Detection
chunks.text:
# Project Write-Up: AI Plant Disease Detection

This is a write-up of the AI Plant Disease Detection project, which I worked on as a team member. It covers what the system does, the data we used, the two models we trained, how we prepared the images, how the model is served to users, and the results.

## What the project does, in simple words

The idea is simple: a person takes a photo of a leaf, and the system tells them whether the plant looks healthy or which illness it most likely has. A farmer or gardener doesn't need to be an expert. They upload a picture, wait under a second, and get an answer on a screen. Catching a sick crop early can save a harvest, so speed and accuracy both matter here.

Under the hood, this is an image classification problem. The computer looks at the colours, spots, edges and textures on a leaf and decides which category the picture belongs to.

## The data

We trained on the PlantVillage dataset, using more than 54,000 leaf images spread across 38 distinct classes. Each class is a combination of a plant and a condition, so the model has to tell apart not just "sick versus healthy" but exactly which disease is showing on which plant. With 38 classes, guessing randomly would be right less than 3% of the time, so the model really has to learn the visual patterns.

chunks.title: Project Write-Up: AI Plant Disease Detection
chunks.text:
We trained on the PlantVillage dataset, using more than 54,000 leaf images spread across 38 distinct classes. Each class is a combination of a plant and a condition, so the model has to tell apart not just "sick versus healthy" but exactly which disease is showing on which plant. With 38 classes, guessing randomly would be right less than 3% of the time, so the model really has to learn the visual patterns.

## Two models: a custom CNN and MobileNetV2

We built the models with TensorFlow and Keras, and we tried two approaches.

**1. A custom convolutional neural network (CNN).** A CNN learns small filters that slide across an image and respond to patterns like edges, blotches and colour changes. Early layers pick up simple shapes, and deeper layers combine them into more meaningful features, such as the ring-shaped spots of a particular leaf disease. Building our own CNN from scratch was a good way to understand what each layer contributes.

**2. Transfer learning with MobileNetV2.** MobileNetV2 is a network that has already been trained on a huge general image collection, so it already "knows" how to see edges, textures and shapes. Instead of starting from zero, we fine-tuned this pre-trained network on our leaf images. It's like hiring someone who already knows how to read and only teaching them a new subject. MobileNetV2 is also designed to be lightweight, which keeps prediction fast.

chunks.title: Project Write-Up: AI Plant Disease Detection
chunks.text:
**2. Transfer learning with MobileNetV2.** MobileNetV2 is a network that has already been trained on a huge general image collection, so it already "knows" how to see edges, textures and shapes. Instead of starting from zero, we fine-tuned this pre-trained network on our leaf images. It's like hiring someone who already knows how to read and only teaching them a new subject. MobileNetV2 is also designed to be lightweight, which keeps prediction fast.

For training we used the Adam optimizer and categorical cross-entropy loss. Adam adjusts the learning rate for each weight automatically, which usually makes training stable without much tuning. Categorical cross-entropy is the standard loss for problems where each image belongs to exactly one of many classes: it punishes the model more when it is confidently wrong.

## Results

Transfer learning clearly won. The MobileNetV2 model reached **94.45% validation accuracy**. Even more striking, it hit **91% accuracy after the very first epoch**. That fast convergence is the whole point of transfer learning: the network already understood images in general, so it only needed a little nudging to understand leaves. A model trained from scratch has to learn everything, including what an edge looks like, before it can be useful.

## Preparing the images

Raw photos come in all sizes and lighting conditions, so we built a preprocessing and augmentation pipeline:

- **Resizing to 224x224 pixels**, the input size MobileNetV2 expects.
- **Normalization**, scaling pixel values into a small consistent range so training is numerically stable.
- **Rotation, flipping and shearing**, which create slightly altered copies of training images.

chunks.title: Project Write-Up: AI Plant Disease Detection
chunks.text:
Raw photos come in all sizes and lighting conditions, so we built a preprocessing and augmentation pipeline:

- **Resizing to 224x224 pixels**, the input size MobileNetV2 expects.
- **Normalization**, scaling pixel values into a small consistent range so training is numerically stable.
- **Rotation, flipping and shearing**, which create slightly altered copies of training images.

Augmentation matters because a model can otherwise memorise the exact training photos instead of learning the general pattern, which is called overfitting. If the model sees the same leaf rotated, mirrored and slightly skewed, it learns that the disease is the spots themselves, not the angle the photo was taken from. This makes it more reliable on new photos taken by real users.

## From model to a usable app

A model sitting in a notebook doesn't help anyone, so we built a full-stack deployment. The trained model is saved as an .h5 file and loaded by a **Flask API** on the backend. The frontend is a **React dashboard** where the user uploads an image. The dashboard sends the image to the Flask API, the API runs it through the model, and the prediction comes back to the screen. Real-time inference takes about **0.8 seconds** per image, which feels instant for the user.

## What this project shows

This project combines machine learning with turning a model into a working product. Technically, the main takeaway is that a strong pre-trained model like MobileNetV2 can reach high accuracy very quickly, instead of reinventing the wheel with a model built from scratch. It also fits the advice I give juniors: build projects that solve significant modern problems, and crop health is one of them.

## Plain summary

In short, our team made a program that looks at pictures of plant leaves and recognises 38 different health conditions. We taught it using tens of thousands of example photos, reused a ready-made vision network to learn faster, got it right about 94 out of 100 times on unseen photos, and wrapped it in a website that gives an answer in under a second.

chunks.title: Project: 3D Food Visualization App
chunks.text:
# Project: 3D Food Visualization App

I was the **team lead** on this project. It is an augmented reality (AR) restaurant platform built with React Native and Expo Router on the frontend, and FastAPI with PostgreSQL on the backend.

## The idea

Menus with tiny photos don't tell you much about what will actually arrive at your table. In this app, a customer scans a QR code at the restaurant and can see a life-size 3D model of a dish sitting right on their table through their phone camera, before ordering it. The 3D dishes are stored in .glb and .usdz formats, which are common 3D model formats for AR on mobile devices.

## Four portals with role-based access

The backend is written in Python with FastAPI and stores data in PostgreSQL. It uses role-based access control (RBAC), which means each type of user only sees and does what their role allows. There are four stakeholder portals:

- **Customer:** browse the menu, view dishes in AR, add to cart, order and pay.
- **Content Admin:** manage the menu and the 3D dish content.
- **Order Manager:** handle incoming orders.
- **Super Admin:** oversee the whole platform.

## Smart inventory

The app tracks inventory in real time. When an ingredient runs out, menu items that depend on it are automatically hidden or disabled, so customers can't order a dish the kitchen can't make.

- **Customer:** browse the menu, view dishes in AR, add to cart, order and pay.
- **Content Admin:** manage the menu and the 3D dish content.
- **Order Manager:** handle incoming orders.
- **Super Admin:** oversee the whole platform.

## Smart inventory

The app tracks inventory in real time. When an ingredient runs out, menu items that depend on it are automatically hidden or disabled, so customers can't order a dish the kitchen can't make.

## Ordering, payments and analytics

I designed the end-to-end ordering flow: menu, cart, checkout and payment. The platform also has built-in analytics that track revenue, ratings, and how many times each dish was viewed in AR, so a restaurant can see which dishes people look at and which ones they actually buy.

## In plain words

This is a phone app for restaurants that lets diners see a realistic, full-size model of their meal on the table before they order. Behind it is a system with separate screens for customers, menu editors, order staff and the owner, which also keeps track of stock and sales.

chunks.title: Project: Cross-Platform Game Hub
chunks.text:
# Project: Cross-Platform Game Hub

The Game Hub is an adaptive, cross-platform collection of games built with React Native, Expo and Expo Router. It started as a mobile-only application, and I turned it into a responsive interface that works on desktop, tablet and mobile.

## Accessibility first

A big part of this project was accessibility. I added:

- **High Contrast mode**
- **XL text**
- **Color-blind modes**
- **Full keyboard navigation**, using number keys 1 to 9 and 1 to 7 to move around without a mouse or touch

Together these reduced usability barriers across 9 app modules.

## Architecture

The hub integrates **chess.js** for the chess game, and I built custom reusable UI components called **AppShell**, **InfoCard** and **AppButton** so every screen looks and behaves consistently. Scores and progress are saved through a centralized **AsyncStorage** service layer, so score tracking and persistence work the same way across all games.

## Better interaction design

Across 7 playable games, I redesigned how the app talks to the player. Disruptive popup alerts were replaced with inline validation and real-time status updates, and I added one-click state recovery with Undo and Restart buttons. Popups interrupt the flow of a game, so it's better to show feedback right where the player is looking.

## In plain words

This is a set of small games that works on phones, tablets and computers. I made it easier to use for people who have trouble seeing colours or small text, or who prefer a keyboard, and I replaced annoying pop-up messages with gentler hints and easy undo buttons.
